title: Husayn refuses
hook: Husayn refuses to give his pledge to Yazid and sets out for Kufa with his family

segments.voice: Yesterday, mulk, rule from Damascus: Mu'awiyah asks for a pledge to his son in advance, and a community that chose its leaders begins to inherit them. Your line was: a dynasty begins. What did you notice being handed on? Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

A messenger knocks in Medina, at night. The governor wants to see Husayn, now. Mu'awiyah is dead, the histories say, and his son Yazid has written: take the pledge from Husayn, and do not let him put it off. Husayn is the younger son of Ali and Fatima, a grandson of the Prophet, peace be upon him. He goes to the governor. He listens. And he asks for time: a pledge like this, he says, should be made in public, before the people, not in a room at night. Then he leaves, and before long he leaves Medina altogether. Today: Husayn refuses.
screen: `A KNOCK AT NIGHT.` → `TAKE THE PLEDGE FROM HUSAYN.` → `NOT IN A ROOM AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: A pledge, a bay'ah, was not a vote. It was a handclasp that bound you to obey. Giving it to Yazid would have meant saying yes to the new shape of power. Husayn would not give it. The histories follow him to Mecca, where he stays near the Kaaba. Then letters start to arrive from Kufa, his father's old city, many letters, the reports say, inviting him to come and lead them. He sends his cousin, Muslim ibn Aqil, ahead to see if the welcome is real. And then, against the advice of relatives and friends who are reported to have begged him to stay, he sets out across the desert. Not with an army. With his family: his sisters, his wives, his children, his brothers, a small circle of companions. Why? Muslims have answered that in different ways. Shia Muslims honor Husayn as the third Imam, and hear in his refusal a stand for the religion itself: that a ruler who did not live by it could not be given the believers' hands. Sunni Muslims honor him as a beloved grandson of the Prophet who refused injustice, though some Sunni scholars held that he should have stayed. Tirmidhi keeps a hadith in which the Prophet says, Husayn is from me, and I am from Husayn. And this is the end of a week. It began at Siffin, with pages on the spears; then the Kharijites, a caliph losing a case over a shield, Ali's death, Hasan's peace, and rule from Damascus. It ends with a man on a road, who would not pledge.
screen: `A PLEDGE WAS A HANDCLASP.` · `LETTERS FROM KUFA.` · `NOT AN ARMY: A FAMILY.` · `HUSAYN IS FROM ME.` · then, large: `HE WOULD NOT PLEDGE.`

segments.voice: The practice: refuse one wrong thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you've been going along with that you know isn't right. A joke at someone's expense. A shortcut at work. A silence when someone is being treated badly. Breathe in. Notice how small the yes has become, how easy. Breathe out. Picture yourself saying no, plainly and without drama, the way Husayn answered the governor: calm, polite, and unmoved. Choose the words you would use. The bell holds the time.
Husayn refuses. The Prophet's grandson would not give his pledge to Yazid, and set out for Kufa with his family. Today's word.
Your line: he would not pledge. Today, say no to one small wrong thing you'd usually let slide, calmly and in the open. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims retell Husayn's refusal to pledge to Yazid as the opening of the Karbala story; Shia Muslims honor him as the third Imam, and Sunni and Shia Muslims alike keep the Prophet's words, Husayn is from me and I am from Husayn.

fork.setup: you're Husayn. the governor calls you in at night and asks for your pledge to Yazid. what do you do?
options: give it quietly and go home.
ask that it be done in public, then leave the city.
refuse loudly and call for a fight.
fork.reveal: he asked for time, saying a pledge belonged in public, and then left Medina for Mecca.

original.note: Arabic: a pledge of allegiance, sealed with a handclasp.

trapdoor: what you thought: Husayn refused because he wanted to be in charge.
what it means: he would not give the binding pledge to Yazid, and set out with his family when Kufa invited him.
what a scholar hears: the bay'ah as a covenant of obedience, Husayn as the third Imam for Shia Muslims, and the hadith in Tirmidhi: Husayn is from me and I am from Husayn.

notes: Tirmidhi 3775 cited from memory; confirm number.
The night summons and Husayn's request that the pledge be made in public follow al-Tabari's account; confirm the framing.
'Many letters, the reports say': al-Tabari and others describe a great number; no count given here. Confirm.
Sentence on Sunni views ('many Sunni Muslims honor him... while some Sunni scholars held that he should have stayed') is a broad claim kept soft; a Keeper should check fairness and wording.
Week-end recap lists days 883–888 by title.

Audit: the practice's simile ('saying no ... the way Husayn asked for the pledge to be made in public') did not make sense, since his request was a deferral, not a no; now 'the way Husayn answered the governor: calm, polite, and unmoved'.

Editor: 'the second grandson' (a count) changed to 'a grandson'; 'Both keep a hadith in Tirmidhi' (Tirmidhi is a Sunni collection) changed to 'Tirmidhi keeps a hadith'; practice said Husayn asked for the pledge 'in daylight', corrected to 'in public' to match the hook.
